blocks.text: Why he joined ossifrages to vultures, as equally devoted to their young, is very well known. For in Oppian, book 1 of the Halieutica, we read that the ossifrage groans and wails like a woman if anyone has stolen one of its chicks, and thereafter does not leave the nest, neglecting food. Nor is it merciful only toward its own chicks, but toward those of others as well. For the chicks cast out by eagles (says Pliny) are taken up by the kindred race of the ossifrage, which rears them with its own. And Antigonus, Story 52: Ὁ δὲ Ἀριστοτέλης φησὶ τὴν φήνην τοὺς ἐκβληθέντας τῶν νεοττῶν ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀετοῦ λαμβάνειν, καὶ ἐκτρέφειν [Ho de Aristotelēs phēsi tēn phēnēn tous ekblēthentas tōn neottōn hypo tou aetou lambanein, kai ektrephein]· Aristotle says that the ossifrage takes up and rears the chicks cast out by the eagle. Namely in History, book 9, chapter 34: Ἡ δὲ καλουμένη φήνη ἐστὶν ἤπιος, καὶ τὰ τέκνα ἐκτρέφει, καὶ τὰ αὐτῆς, καὶ τὰ τοῦ ἀετοῦ [Hē de kaloumenē phēnē estin ēpios, kai ta tekna ektrephei, kai ta autēs, kai ta tou aetou]· The bird called phene (that is, the ossifrage) is kindly, and besides its own it also rears the chicks of the eagle. Ἤπιος [ēpios] here is the same as pius [devoted, kindly], and refers to devotion and mercy toward the chicks it rears, so that it is almost the same as רחום rachum. So Paul uses it in 1 Thessal. II, 7: Ἐγενήθημεν, he says, ἤπιοι ἐν μέσω ὑμῶν, ὡς ἂν τροφὸς θάλπῃ τὰ ἑαυτῆς τέκνα [Egenēthēmen ēpioi en mesō hymōn, hōs an trophos thalpē ta heautēs tekna]. Thus there is a great similarity of habits between the vulture and the ossifrage. Hence it came about that the Philosopher in the book of Marvels, and Pliny following him, asserts that vultures are begotten from ossifrages. And not a few count the ossifrage among the species of vultures, among them the Kiranides, Gesner and Dalechamp: just as we have already said that some of the Arabs interpret رخمة [rakhama] rachamam, instead of vulture, as ossifrage. Meanwhile it is already clear from this that Diodorus of Tarsus is gravely mistaken when he writes that vultures οὐ τρέφειν τὰ γεννήματα [ou trephein ta gennēmata], do not rear their offspring: unless by the name vultures he means eagles; although even of eagles it is not simply true, as we have shown in its place ^{e)}.

The vulture's clemency and kindness also appears most clearly from the fact that it protects not only its own offspring but also other birds from the hawk, if we believe Cassiodorus [III, 76], book 2, Letter 19. Alas! he says, devotion is found in birds which is abandoned by the human condition. The vulture itself, whose life is the carcass of another, a body of such great size, is not shown to be hostile even to small birds: rather it strikes with its wings the hawk that pursues the life of feathered birds, tears it with its beak, and strives with its whole weight to come to the aid of those in danger. And a little later, dealing with slaves who had killed their master: Let him therefore become the food of the devoted vulture, who could cruelly desire the death of his shepherd. You see, reader, that the vulture is called devoted and set forth as an example of devotion, as one that takes into its protection not only its own chicks but any birds whatever, [col. 320] so as to keep them safe and sound from every danger as far as it can. Pliny writes something similar of the kestrel, book 10, chapter 37: The kestrel defends doves and terrifies hawks by a natural power, so much that they flee its sight and its voice.
